processing: Ripe pu-erh made by wet piling and selected or sold for a jujube-like aroma. No agreed standard method is documented; aroma in shu is shaped by material, processing, grade and storage.
harvest_season: No defined season; as usual for ripe pu-erh, it is often a blend and sold by production year.
appearance_dry: Dark reddish-brown leaf, loose, pressed or in nuggets depending on the maker.
appearance_liquor: Deep, clear red-brown, as is typical of ripe pu-erh.
taste_profile: Smooth and sweet, with an aroma compared to dried red dates (jujube) over the usual aged, woody notes of shu.

brewing.notes: Rinse once or twice. Very hot water brings out the sweet aroma; a clean-smelling pot or gaiwan makes it easier to pick up.

vintage_note: Sold by production year like other ripe pu-erh, as cakes, bricks, loose leaf or nuggets. Most is drunk within about ten years. Aroma in stored shu tends to deepen with time, so a tea with a few years of rest may show more of this note.
description:
Zao xiang means jujube fragrance. It is less a type of tea than a description of an aroma: one of the classic scents people look for in ripe pu-erh, alongside aged and sticky-rice notes.

There is no defined recipe behind the label. Research on ripe pu-erh aroma points to a mixture of compounds formed in piling and storage, with material, process, grade and storage all shifting the result. Nothing settled ties this particular note to one cause, so be sceptical of confident explanations.

In the cup, look for the warm sweetness of dried red dates over a smooth, woody, low-bitterness body. It tends to come through clearly with very hot water, and a heavy-handed steep can hide it under the dark, earthy notes.

Since anyone can print the word on a wrapper, trust your nose. A natural date note is soft and sits within the tea; a loud candy-like smell may suggest flavouring. Try it beside a plain shu from the same maker to find out whether the label means anything.
history: Little is documented about when zao xiang came into use as a selling term. It belongs to the vocabulary of aroma used for ripe pu-erh, a tea type that itself depends on wet piling, and no individual producer or date is established as its origin.
